PLANT THE MOON CHALLENGE - SPRING 2025 
Enhancing Spinach Growth and Yield in Lunar Regolith using 
Nano supplement against Salt Stress 
Introduction 
As humanity sets its sights on long-term lunar exploration and habitation, one of the key 
questions must answer is: Can we grow food on the Moon? This season, VAIAL Team 4 took 
on this exciting challenge by investigating how spinach, a nutrient-rich leafy green, grows in a 
simulated lunar environment using the lunar regolith. 
By experimenting with regolith simulant, this experiment aimed to understand the possibilities 
and limitations of cultivating crops in space-like conditions. This project not only explored the 
viability of spinach as a lunar crop but also contributed to the broader mission of sustainable 
space agriculture. This report give the new insight into the space agriculture, innovation, and 
unexpected discoveries behind the experience to grow spinach on the Moon. 
Spinach is a promising crop for cultivation in lunar conditions using treated lunar regolith as a 
growth medium. Its adaptability to hydroponic and controlled-environment farming makes it 
suitable for space habitats where soil is limited. When supplemented with essential nutrients 
and organic matter, lunar regolith can support spinach growth, providing a sustainable source 
of vitamins A, C, K, iron, and folate for astronauts. Spinach’s short growth cycle, efficient 
space use, and potential for contributing to oxygen production and psychological well-being 
make it an ideal candidate for lunar agriculture. 
Theory: 
The ability to sustain crop growth using lunar regolith is essential for the success of long-term 
lunar missions. Given the immense logistical challenges and costs associated with transporting 
materials from Earth, utilizing in-situ resources—such as lunar regolith—for agriculture is 
critical. However, previous studies have demonstrated that unmodified lunar regolith lacks 
essential nutrients and possesses inadequate structural characteristics for effective plant 
cultivation. 
Lunar regolith contains various salts such as silicates, oxides, sodium, potassium and calcium 
(Zhou et al., 2024). The detailed report of lunar soil element analysis was given in Table (1). 
The salts present in the lunar regolith may create salt stress and it is different from the earth

soil salinity. The presence of salt forming elements in lunar regolith plays a significant impact 
on crop growth and yield. With this reason, salt stress of lunar regolith considered as a problem 
in the present study. 
Table 1. Lunar regolith chemical properties (Initial soil analysis) 
 
The previous experiments investigated the feasibility of growing crops in lunar regolith that 
was modified to mimic the texture and nutrient composition of loamy Earth soil. A 52:48 ratio 
of lunar regolith to additive was used to create a growth medium, in which four crop species 
were cultivated over a seven-week period. Among the species tested, Fagopyrum esculentum 
(buckwheat) exhibited significantly higher biomass in the modified lunar regolith compared to 
the Earth soil control (Thorsen et al., 2023). In the present study, similar potting media was 
prepared using the amendments (50%) with regolith (50%) and to combat the problems of lunar 
simulant (Table 2). 
Spinach is a familiar test crop and sensitive to the daylength (photoperiod) and used to test 
under various abiotic stresses. Recent report on Spinach showed potential ability to overcome 
the salinity stress under LED lights (Vajjiravel et al., 2024). This review reasoned for the 
selection of Spinach as a test crop and modified photoperiod as a treatment in the current study. 
The findings of Thorsen and co-workers (2023) suggest that the crop cultivation on the Moon 
may be achievable using lunar regolith supplemented with a relatively small amount of additive 
material. With this background, the current study was formulated that the nano materials (nano 
particle and nanotubes) supplementation to reduce the salt stress of lunar regolith. This study 
aimed to use the resource-efficient inputs (modified amendments, day length and nano material 
supplementation) could increase food production in extra-terrestrial environments.

soil mixtures and 12 pots containing Earth soil mixtures (Figure 1.). Each group is further 
divided into control and treatment conditions, with four replications per condition to ensure 
accuracy and reliability in the results. The media composition of individual pots given below 
(Table 2.).

Table 3. Overview of treatment details 
 
In this experiment, Spinach seeds are grown separately in pots containing either Earth soil or 
lunar soil to compare their growth performance, with a major focus on salt stress. Both soil 
types receive the same amendments in equal proportions to maintain consistency. There were 
twenty seeds of Spinach (UGAOO green spinach, Ugaoo Agritech Pvt Ltd, Pune) were sown 
in the pots. The lunar soil pots with seeds were kept in a plant growth chamber under a light 
cycle of 12 hours of light followed by a dark period. The daylength of light increased to 14 
hours on every five days that simulating increased daylength available in moon. However, on 
every fifth day, the control pots in the lunar soil kept for 12 hours light cycle. The earth soil 
pots with seeds were kept in the controlled greenhouse and maintained under natural daylength. 
Each pots were irrigated manually on every day and the volume of water increased by 30% 
more after the measurement of drainage water. To ensure proper nutrient supply, NPK 
(19:19:19) is fertigated for every pot twice a week at a rate of 1g/L of Water. 
The silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) were supplemented to the pots 
of both soil after 15 days of sowing. Silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) play a significant role in 
enhancing plant growth and may have potential to alleviate salinity stress. The SiNPs were 
biosynthesized from the biodynamic manure 501 (Bharathy and Parthasarathi, 2025) and 
procured from Dr. Parthasarathi’s research lab, VAIAL, VIT. Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer 
several benefits in promoting plant growth and possible to alleviate salinity stress. The 
commercially available CNTs were purchased from the market used for supplementation.

 Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) help alleviate plant stress by improving the soil-like 
medium’s water retention, nutrient availability, and overall plant compatibility. CNTs 
act as nano-scale soil conditioners, enhancing the physical properties of regolith to 
support better root growth and moisture absorption. Functionalized CNTs can also serve 
as carriers for nutrients or plant growth regulators, delivering them efficiently to plants 
growing in this hostile medium. 
 Silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) improve plant water uptake by enhancing root structure 
and increasing the expression of aquaporins, which are water channel proteins. They 
also help regulate ion homeostasis by reducing toxic sodium uptake and promoting the 
selective absorption of essential ions like potassium and calcium. Furthermore, SiNPs 
boost the plant's antioxidant defense system, reducing oxidative damage caused by 
stress-related reactive oxygen species (ROS). 
Methodology 
Growth Parameters: 
The morphological data of plant height (cm), leaf length (cm), leaf breadth (cm) and no of 
leaves from each pots were collected from three tagged plants on week 3, week 5, week 7. For 
checking the parameters ruler was used to measure. For earth soil also the same 
procedure is followed. 
Physiological parameters 
1. Select Representative Plants 
 Choose 3–5 representative plants per treatment or plot. 
 Label them to ensure the same plants are used each week. 
2. Select Leaves for Measurement 
 Use fully expanded, healthy leaves—typically the youngest fully developed 
leaf. 
 Select 3–5 leaves per plant. 
 Avoid damaged, diseased, or shaded leaves. 
3. Measurement Timing 
 Perform measurements weekly, preferably: 
 At the same time of day (morning is best to avoid heat stress effects).

Net photosynthetic rate: 
 By using the average spade meter value of each treatments and apply it in the Net 
Photosynthetic Rate (NPR) formulae to find out the NPR : 
 NPR=0.0049(x²)+ 0.0383(x) - 4.1593 
Stomatal conductance: 
By using the average spade meter value of each treatments and apply it in the Stomatal 
Conductance (SC) formulae to find out the SC : 
 SC=0.0027(x²)+ 0.00214(x)+ 0.0808 
Transpiration rate: 
By using the average spade meter value of each treatments and apply it in Transpiration Rate 
(T) formulae to find out the T : 
 T=0.0094(x²)+ 0.1627(x) + 1.0563 
Metabolite analysis 
Plants from each treatment and control group were harvested and kept separately. The samples 
were first shade-dried and then oven-dried at 60°C for one day. The dried plant material was 
then ground into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle. 
From each finely powdered plant sample, 100 mg was taken and mixed with 5 mL of methanol. 
The mixture was placed in a shaker at 100 rpm and left overnight. 
The following day, the samples were subjected to sonication and then returned to the shaker 
for an additional 5 to 6 hours. After shaking, the extracts were transferred to petri plates and 
oven-dried. 
The dried residue was carefully scraped and transferred into Eppendorf tubes. These samples 
were then sent to the GC Analysis Lab at Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, for 
Gas Chromatography (GC) analysis. 
Harvest analysis 
The plants were harvested, and roots were removed from the potted soil on Week 7. The fresh 
yield of Spinach was measured pot wise. The root length was measured by selecting 3 plants 
randomly from each pot and noted. After all the measurements, samples were first shade-dried

and then oven-dried at 60°C for one day. After drying, the dry weight of each sample was 
recorded. The dried plant material was then ground into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle. 
From each powdered sample, 1 gram was packed and sent for Inductively Coupled Plasma 
(ICP) analysis to the National Agro Foundation, Chennai. 
Nutrient analysis 
An initial sample of 200 grams of lunar regolith was collected, packed securely, and sent for 
Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) analysis to the National Agro Foundation, Chennai 
Soil samples were collected from all 24 pots separately for each treatment, both from the lunar 
and earth soils. The collected soil was sieved to obtain fine particles suitable for analysis. 
From each sample, 200 grams of sieved soil was measured and oven-dried at 60°C for 8 hours 
to remove moisture. The dried soil samples were then carefully packed and sent for Inductively 
Coupled Plasma (ICP) analysis to the National Agro Foundation, Chennai. 
Results and Discussion 
Spinach cultivated in lunar regolith exhibited superior growth (Fig 2a.) performance of plant 
height, leaf numbers, leaf dimensions compared to those grown in Earth soil samples, 
particularly during the 3rd and 5th weeks of observation. This enhanced growth is notably 
attributed to the application of Silica nanoparticles (SiNPs), which likely increased the 
antioxidant enzymatic activity, i.e. lipid peroxidation (Figure 4.) and regulate the nutrient 
uptake under salt stress condition (Alam et al., 2022). The control samples of lunar soil showed 
lower growth performance similar to the study report of Paul et al (2022) and reasoned due to 
slow crop establishment lead to severe stress morphologies. By the 7th week, the Spinach 
height, leaf length (Fig. 2b.) was increased by SiNPs followed by carbon nanotubes (CNTs) 
due to enhanced phosphorous and carbon use from the soil. As a result of nanoparticle 
supplementation, the leaf photosynthetic surface will be increased. 
Leaf photosynthesis is a complex process which was mainly affected by salt stress due to 
reduced water potential and excessive salt toxic ions in the root zone of the crop. This was 
reasoned for the reduced photosynthetic performance and leaf chlorophyll content in the 
control samples of Lunar soil. The leaf chlorophyll content (SPAD), net photosynthetic rate, 
stomatal conductance and transpiration rate values are significantly higher in lunar soil + SiNPs 
treatment during week 4 and showed consistent leaf physiology during week 6 (Fig 3a, 3b.). 
Higher SPAD chlorophyll content with SiNPs supplementation increase the gene expression of

photosystem machinery and associated signalling pathway of chlorophyll biosynthesis 
(Lesharadevi et al., 2022). The long daylength can reduce the leaf photosynthesis than the short 
day (SD) plants (Xu et al., 2022). In contrast, the SiNPs and CNTs supplement can alter the 
long daylength effect by showcasing better photosynthetic performance in lunar soil.

The lipid peroxidation levels may indicate the osmotic stress damage caused by lipid 
peroxidation. This found to be highest in the control treatments of lunar soil. In contrast, the 
application of nanomaterials particularly carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and silica nanoparticles 
(SiNPs) significantly reduced lipid peroxidation across both lunar and Earth soil samples (Fig 
4.). This reduction highlights the effectiveness of these nanomaterials in safeguarding plant cell 
membranes, mitigating damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), and enhancing the 
overall salt stress tolerance of the plants.

Interestingly, silica nanoparticles (LT2) demonstrated better fresh yield and total dry mass in 
lunar regolith by reducing salt stress more effectively, while carbon nanotubes showed greater 
efficacy in Earth soil conditions (Fig. 5.). These observations emphasize the critical role of 
nanoparticle in advancing sustainable cultivation, particularly in challenging extraterrestrial 
environments, by boosting plant resilience and minimizing stress-induced cellular damage. 
Similar yield response observed in cherry radish with increased yield and nutritional quality by 
the Si-based nanomaterial (Xu et al., 2023).

The metabolomics of Spinach leaves showed a variety of chemical structures with diverse 
functional groups. The GC images of LT2, LT1 and LC shows a clear increase in metabolites 
in the shoot of spinach which indicated the SiNPs and CNTs alter the metabolic profile (Fig 
7.). The CNTs altered the metabolome of the plant and subsequently enhanced plant growth 
which was in accordance with the previous report of Chen et al., (2022). Similarly, Xi et al. 
(2023) reported that SiNPs resulted in significant separation metabolic profile in cherry radish 
plants. 
A significant reduction in root length was observed in the control treatment of lunar soil which 
has also been observed under high osmotic stress (Shrivastava and Kumar, 2015). However, in 
the same soil media, the SiNPs were increase the root length which attributed to differential 
response to salt stress. In addition, the SiNPs increase the uptake of important elements Ca, 
Mg and K levels by maintain the intercellular ionic balance. In the lunar control (LC) plants 
the ionic ratio analysis exhibited poor ionic balance. i.e. Na/K ratio (0.24), Na/Ca (2.91) and 
Na/Mg (1.89) (Table 4.). Among the treated lunar samples, L1 and L2 showed higher ratios of 
Na/K, Na/Ca and Na/Mg. This suggests that the application of treatments such as silica 
nanoparticles and carbon nanotubes helped to mitigate salt stress, which could have been 
significantly higher in the absence of such amendments.

The lunar regolith samples, especially LT2 exhibited significantly lower Na/K (0.33), along 
with moderate Na/Ca and Na/Mg ratios (Fig 5.), suggesting effective mitigation of sodium 
toxicity due to the application of silica nanoparticles and carbon nanotubes. These results 
indicate that the use of nanomaterial treatments was more effective in lunar regolith that 
enhancing the plant’s ability to regulate ion balance and maintain better physiological function 
under potentially stressful conditions.

Conclusion: 
The experiment successfully demonstrates that lunar regolith, when appropriately amended and 
supplemented with nanomaterials like silica nanoparticles and carbon nanotubes, can support 
the healthy and vigorous growth of spinach. Among the treatments, silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) 
yielded the most favorable results in terms of plant height, root development, nutrient uptake, 
salinity stress mitigation, and physiological activity. 
While Earth soil showed delayed adaptation under the same treatments, lunar regolith 
responded robustly, marking it as a promising medium for lunar agriculture. The results 
reinforce the SiNPs showed better ionic balance, osmoregulation, membrane stability and stress 
tolerance and yield of spinach under lunar soil and lunar daylength. The carbon nanotubes 
(CNTs) and Silica nano particles (SiNPs) supplementation recommended for lunar soil 
amendment to achieve better growth and yield. In order to reduce salt stress and enhance 
development and production, silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) have been recommended as lunar 
soil amendments.This nanomaterials are the viable, right amendments and environmental 
control, can play a pivotal role in ensuring food security in the off-world habitats.
